pairs.reply1:
He uses it as an example of an early computer that was analogue, not digital. It is a historical illustration, and it is not a proof. He says the earliest computers were not digital Turing machines but analogue devices operating in continuous time [spya-zg9me8]. That claim sits inside his second argument, "Other Games In Town". The argument is that Turing-style computation is only one kind, and that other kinds of dynamics and function lie beyond it [spya-gw0hsq]. The mechanism is the oldest case in a short history that continues with 1950s cybernetics and then neuromorphic and "mortal" computation [spya-zg9me8 spya-kjfjgm]. That history sets up his claim that these alternatives are less substrate-flexible than digital computation [spya-kjfjgm].

One detail in the passage looks wrong. The article dates the mechanism to "around 2,000 BCE" [spya-zg9me8]. Sources I found give a date about 2,000 years ago. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antikythera_mechanism) lists it as made in the 2nd century BC, and the [World History Encyclopedia](https://www.worldhistory.org/Antikythera_Mechanism/) dates it to roughly 205–60 BCE. My inference is that "2,000 BCE" is a slip for "2,000 years ago". It doesn't affect his point.
pairs.reply2:
He uses it as an early example of computation that isn't digital Turing computation. The article says the earliest computers were analogue devices working in continuous time, not digital Turing machines. The Antikythera mechanism is its first illustration, and the article follows it with cybernetics in the 1950s.

The example sits in the "Other Games In Town" section. That section argues that Turing algorithms are powerful, but many kinds of dynamics and functions go beyond them. The mechanism is a reminder that "computation" has not always meant Turing-style algorithms. This sets up the point that alternative forms of computation are more closely tied to their material basis, and so less substrate-flexible, than standard digital computation. That supports the essay's wider case against computational functionalism, the view that the right computation is enough for consciousness.

The article dates the mechanism to around 2,000 BCE. The article doesn't say so, but my recollection is that it is usually dated to roughly the second century BCE. I haven't verified that, so check it before relying on either date. The date doesn't affect the argument.

input.said: He goes after Chalmers' neural replacement thing, where you swap neurons for silicon one at a time. And he says it, um, fails at the first hurdle, because you can't actually replace any bit of a brain with a perfect silicon copy — so it doesn't show consciousness is substrate independent.

articleBlocks.text: This reveals the weakness of the popular “neural replacement” thought experiment, most commonly associated with Chalmers, which invites us to imagine progressively replacing brain parts with silicon equivalents that function in exactly the same way as their biological counterparts. The supposed conclusion is that properties like cognition and consciousness must be substrate independent (or at least silicon-substrate-flexible). This thought experiment has become a prominent trope in discussions of artificial consciousness, usually invoked to support its possibility. Hinton recently appealed to it in just this way, in an interview where he claimed that conscious AI was already with us. But the argument fails at its first hurdle, given the impossibility of replacing any part of the brain with a perfect silicon equivalent.

pairs.facts: Chalmers' fading/dancing qualia argument (1995/96) is a well-known defence of organizational invariance; whether a perfect functional replacement is possible in practice is disputed; Seth's rejection is one side of a live debate.

pairs.reply1:
Seth says the thought experiment fails at the start, because its key premise can't be met. The argument asks us to imagine replacing brain parts one at a time with silicon parts that work in exactly the same way, and to conclude that consciousness doesn't depend on the material. He says it "fails at its first hurdle," since no part of the brain can be swapped for a perfect silicon equivalent [spya-ahtr6e]. He also notes that Hinton recently used it to claim conscious AI is already here [spya-ahtr6e].

His reason comes just before this. Real brains are tightly integrated across scales, so you can't assume one neuron can be replaced by a silicon version that keeps its input-output behavior exactly the same [spya-jnwfxp]. His example is work by Chintaluri and Vogels, who found that some neurons fire to clear metabolic waste. Replacing those would mean building a silicon metabolism too, and he says silicon isn't suited to that [spya-un9fjn]. His conclusion is that the only perfect replacement for a biological neuron is another biological neuron [spya-un9fjn].

My inference is that this fits his broader aim. The thought experiment assumes the substrate (the physical material) doesn't matter, which is the point he is contesting in this section. His case that brains can't cleanly separate what they do from what they are [spya-zw2m7u] would make that assumption look circular.

The article doesn't say how Chalmers or others have answered this objection. If you want that, I can search for it.
pairs.reply2:
Seth thinks the thought experiment fails because its starting premise can't be met. He says it "fails at its first hurdle," since no part of the brain could be swapped for a perfect silicon equivalent [spya-ahtr6e]. In the same passage he describes the experiment as asking us to replace brain parts step by step with silicon parts that work identically. The supposed conclusion is that cognition and consciousness don't depend on what the brain is made of. He also notes that Hinton recently used it to argue conscious AI is already here [spya-ahtr6e].

His reason comes just before. Real brains are tightly integrated across scales, which he calls "generative entrenchment." So you can't assume a single neuron could be replaced by a silicon one while keeping its input-output behavior exactly the same [spya-jnwfxp]. His example is work by Chintaluri and Vogels, who found that some neurons fire spikes apparently to clear metabolic waste. A perfect silicon stand-in would need its own silicon-based metabolism, which he says silicon isn't suited for [spya-un9fjn].

My inference is that he isn't saying the reasoning is invalid. The experiment assumes the replacement preserves function perfectly, and he denies that this can happen. This also ties to his first argument, that brains aren't computers because what they do can't be separated from what they are [spya-zw2m7u].

pairs.facts: Nothing in this passage is known to be wrong or seriously disputed; McCulloch & Pitts 1943; Nagel 1974 'What is it like to be a bat?'.
pairs.reply1:
He says McCulloch and Pitts showed in a landmark paper that networks of highly simplified abstract neurons can perform logical operations [spya-va8qxr]. The claim that such networks could in principle run any algorithm comes from later work, by Kleene among others. That work showed the networks were "Turing complete" once given a tape-like memory, as in a Turing machine [spya-va8qxr]. So the "any algorithm" result isn't credited to McCulloch and Pitts themselves. Figure 2's caption shows what their simplified neuron does: it sums weighted inputs and outputs a 1 or a 0 [spya-qknqjx].

Seth uses this to set up his first argument, that brains are not computers. He pairs the result with Turing's work and calls the pair a "mathematical marriage of convenience." You can treat brains as simple networks and ignore their messy biology, and in return you get everything Turing computation offers [spya-v5vz2t]. Today's artificial neural networks are the "children" of that marriage [spya-va72zk].

He then argues the marriage "starts to fall apart" if what brains do can't be separated from what they physically are [spya-p4vmm0]. The McCulloch-Pitts result is therefore the foundation he is arguing against, not a point he disputes.
pairs.reply2:
He says McCulloch and Pitts showed that networks of highly simplified abstract neurons can perform logical operations [spya-va8qxr]. The "Turing complete" result isn't theirs. It came from later work, by Kleene among others, which showed that such networks, once given a tape-like memory, could in principle run any algorithm [spya-va8qxr]. The Figure 2 caption shows what one of these simplified neurons does: it weights its inputs, sums them and produces an output [spya-qknqjx].

In the argument, this result is half of what he calls a "mathematical marriage of convenience." Brains can be treated as simple networks of abstract neurons, which brings in everything Turing computation offers [spya-v5vz2t]. He says today's artificial neural networks descend directly from this work [spya-va72zk]. This sets up his first argument. If you can't separate what a brain does from what it physically is, the marriage starts to fall apart [spya-p4vmm0].

input.said: He says consciousness is about being rather than doing, and he uses Nagel's line, that something's conscious if there's something it is like to be it.

articleBlocks.text: Consciousness, in contrast to intelligence, is mostly about being. Half a century ago, the philosopher Thomas Nagel famously offered that “an organism has conscious mental states if and only if there is something it is like to be that organism.” Consciousness is the difference between normal wakefulness and the oblivion of deep general anesthesia. It is the experiential aspect of brain function and especially of perception: the colors, shapes, tastes, emotions, thoughts and more, that give our lives texture and meaning. The blueness of the sky on a clear day. The bitter tang and headrush of your first coffee.

Seth names this thought experiment, which he associates with Chalmers, and says it fails: "the argument fails at its first hurdle, given the impossibility of replacing any part of the brain with a perfect silicon equivalent" [spya-ahtr6e]. His reason is that a neuron is not a simple input-output device that could be swapped out. Some neurons fire spikes of activity apparently to clear metabolic waste, so a perfect silicon stand-in "would require inventing a whole new silicon-based metabolism, too" [spya-un9fjn]. For that reason he thinks the only seamless replacement for a biological neuron is another biological neuron. The premise that the swap leaves everything unchanged is therefore where he says the argument breaks.
